div.head: II Atr 3
div.ab: ⁊ ælc agenra friðmanna frið hæbbe, ge on lande ge on wætere, ge binnan muðan ge butan.
Et omnis friðmannus noster pacem habeat in terris et aquis, et intra portum et extra.
[Be ðæs cyninges fryþmannum.] ⁊ ælc agenra friðmanna frið hæbbe, ge on lande ge on wætere, ge binnan muðan ge butan.

(Von Leuten aus des Königs Friedensgebiet. Ld) Und jeder der Leute, die selbst jenem Frieden[sgebiete dieses Vertrages] angehören, geniesse Friedensschutz, sowohl zu Lande wie zu Wasser, sowohl in der Flussmündung wie draussen.

(Of men from the king's peace-area. Ld) And let every one of the men who themselves belong to that peace[-area of this treaty] enjoy protection, both on land and on water, both within the estuary and outside.
But all of those who are specially included in the truce are to enjoy the protection of the truce, whether on land or on water, whether within an estuary or not.
And each of the men to whom the truce applies is to have peace both on land and on water, both within the estuary and outside.

note.seg: Be ðæs cyninges fryþmannum überschr. Ld
Be ðæs cyninges fryþmannum as heading in Ld
The rubric belongs more properly to 3, 1

Neuere, auch Pollock 78, verstehen ‘Engländer’. Q aber meint vielleicht mit noster ‘unser beider’, der Vertragschliesser. Nur dies ist richtig; so auch Worsaae 251. Denn dass der Engländer im Englischen Hafen Schutz genoss, ist selbstverständlich; und wo offenbar dieser allein im folgenden Satz 3, 1 Subjekt ist, heisst er ‘friðman König Æthelreds (s. o. 2³)’, nicht einfach ‘er’, wie doch bei jener Annahme natürlich wäre. Agen steht also im weiteren Sinne beider Verbündeten, in Ggs. zu unfriðscip des Neutralen in 2³

Recent scholars, including Pollock 78, understand ‘Englishman’. Q, however, perhaps means by noster ‘of us both’, i.e. of the contracting parties. Only this is correct; so too Worsaae 251. For it goes without saying that the Englishman enjoyed protection in an English harbour; and where he is evidently the sole subject, in the following sentence 3, 1, he is called ‘King Æthelred’s friðman (see above 2³)’, not simply ‘he’, as would surely be natural on that assumption. Agen thus stands in the wider sense of both allies, in contrast to the unfriðscip of the neutral in 2³
omnis friðmannus noster, Q, probably including both parties, cf. the following clause, Æthelredes cynges friðman.
